name: Curse of knowledge
statement: Once someone knows a thing they cannot set it aside, so they overestimate how much of it other people already know.
meaning: The claim is about a subtraction that people cannot perform. Judging what a less informed person believes means holding your own knowledge out of the calculation, and the finding is that the knowledge leaks back in. Camerer, Loewenstein and Weber wrote the leak down formally. A forecaster with information I1 should report E(X|I0) when asked what someone holding only I0 expects; instead they report a weighted blend of E(X|I0) and E(X|I1), and the weight on their own richer information is the size of the bias. The same structure covers hindsight bias, where the naive perspective being reconstructed is the person's own earlier one, and false-belief reasoning, where it belongs to somebody else.

origin.who: Colin Camerer, George Loewenstein and Martin Weber
origin.note: The paper names the effect and credits the phrase to Robin Hogarth in a footnote. It treats the phenomenon as already established in psychology, citing Fischhoff's 1975 hindsight work, and asks the economic question instead: whether incentives, feedback and markets clear the bias away.

evidence: The economics experiment ran in two stages. In the first, 51 Wharton students read Value Line reports and predicted eight companies' 1980 earnings. In the second, run two months later, groups of nine experienced traders saw the identical reports with the actual 1980 earnings filled in, then traded assets whose dividend was the first group's mean prediction. Pricing the asset correctly required ignoring the true earnings. Equilibrium prices settled between the no-bias and full-bias predictions, and the authors report rejecting both hypotheses strongly. Judgements by individuals given incentives (n = 19) or incentives plus feedback (n = 13) showed more bias than judgements made inside the markets, which the paper summarises as markets halving the bias without removing it. Feedback on its own did nothing. The famous demonstration is a different study and is described below.

replication.headline: Two large replication efforts disagree. Seven experiments on 3,074 people put the false-belief effect at d = 0.20, which their authors call a failure to replicate, and three later experiments on 1,308 people put it at d = 0.314.
replication.detail: Birch and Bloom gave 155 Yale undergraduates a displacement task about a girl called Vicki and her violin, and asked for percentage probabilities rather than a yes or no. Knowing where the violin had gone raised ratings for the plausible wrong container from 23% to 34%, d = 0.472, and lowered ratings for the correct container from 71% to 59%, d = 0.459. Knowing an implausible location produced no reliable bias. Ryskin and Brown-Schmidt repeated that experiment seven times with a combined 3,074 participants. Pooling across the seven, the knowledge effect came out at d = 0.20 against the original 0.469, and the plausibility effect at d = 0.24 against the original 0.645. Those two baselines are their own figures for the original data, which is why 0.469 sits beside the 0.472 printed by Birch and Bloom. Two of the seven runs found the knowledge effect at p < .05, with a third at p = .053. Their own test is that the original design, with about 50 people per condition, had roughly 17% power to detect d = 0.20, so the results are substantively different rather than a quiet confirmation. Farrar and Ostojić then ran the task again on 283, 281 and 744 people, varying whether the protagonist was an in-group member, an out-group member or a dog. Their meta-analysis of the three put the knowledge effect at d = 0.314 across all conditions and at d = 0.407 for the in-group protagonist, rising to d = 0.507 when computed from raw ratings the way Birch and Bloom computed theirs. They read the in-group figure as directly in line with the original. Their containers differed in shape rather than colour, so these are conceptual replications rather than repeats. What holds up sits elsewhere too. Tullis and Feder had participants study trivia questions and estimate what percentage of novices would know each answer. Across four experiments, when participants had to answer the question themselves first, studying the facts damaged both the calibration and the resolution of those estimates.

study.cite: Ryskin, R. A., & Brown-Schmidt, S. (2014). Do adults show a curse of knowledge in false-belief reasoning? A robust estimate of the true effect size. PLoS ONE, 9(3), e92406.

limits: The demonstration everyone quotes was never peer reviewed. Elizabeth Newton's tappers and listeners study is a chapter of her 1990 Stanford doctoral dissertation, and no journal version of it appears in Crossref or in the searches run for this entry. The dissertation was read directly for these figures, and they hold up. 80 undergraduates were paired, and tappers chose three songs each from a list of 25. Tappers put the chance their listener had named the tune at a mean of 50%, range 10 to 95. Listeners scored 3 hits in 120 tries, 2.5%, outside the entire range of the tappers' guesses. The dissertation contradicts itself on that count, giving two of 150 in the abstract and three of 150 in the discussion, against the three of 120 in the results and in the table. The title is also usually got wrong; it is "The rocky road from actions to intentions", not the "Heard and unheard melodies" phrase attached to it in retellings. No replication of the tapping study was located. No effect size is quoted from the economics paper, which reports a bias index rather than a standardised effect. Guilbault and colleagues' meta-analysis of hindsight bias sits behind a paywall that these checks did not pass. Its pooled estimate was later obtained from the published abstract while writing this site's hindsight-bias entry, and is quoted there rather than here. Searches covered Crossref, PubMed, PLOS, Google via web search, and the full text of the five papers held.
misreadings: The tapping figures get quoted as though 50 against 2.5 were the measured size of the curse of knowledge in general. They are one demonstration, in one unpublished study, of a task listeners find close to impossible, and the gap partly measures the difficulty of the task rather than the tappers' egocentrism. Newton's own listeners guessed that only 3% of an audience would name a tune, so the effect is specific to knowing the tune, not a general optimism. The curse is also treated as a fixed trait of experts, where Camerer and colleagues found market experience cut it by about half within a single session. And it is used interchangeably with hindsight bias, which is one case of it: the naive perspective being reconstructed there is the judge's own earlier one.
